intent: Round-6 architecture recommendation, ruling 2: a circuit breaker on the LLM endpoint. Built as what this process actually needs and can prove: a bounded admission gate per gateway endpoint inside the runtime every caller shares.
reasons: Sits inside HermesRuntime.fetchJson, the one path every gateway request/response call takes; a fault here touches dispatch, chat, composer, research and the reconciler at once.
invariants: I1 Per endpoint, at most PS_GATEWAY_MAX_INFLIGHT request/response calls are in flight; at most PS_GATEWAY_MAX_QUEUE wait, for at most PS_GATEWAY_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_MS. Junk in the environment never disables the gate.
I2 Beyond the limits a call is refused with a 503 that names the gate, the endpoint and the counts. Saturation is a refusal, never a hang.
I3 A slot is released on completion and on throw, and handed straight to the next waiter, first in first out.
I4 One saturated endpoint cannot starve another. The gate is keyed by base URL.
I5 Streams hold no slot. An SSE subscription is open for the life of a run; the gate is for the calls that pile up.
I6 The gate publishes a snapshot, and the process has exactly one gate, on globalThis, the way the scheduler singleton lives.
why_a_gate_and_not_a_breaker: A classic breaker trips open on an error rate and then refuses everything for a cooling period, which for a single-operator control plane means a gateway that hiccups once locks the operator out for the length of the window. The failure round 6 actually saw was a gateway that stopped keeping up: requests piling into it, callers waiting on it, and the healthy profile behind the same runtime waiting too. A per-endpoint admission gate answers exactly that, degrades to a named 503 instead of a cliff, and recovers the instant the gateway answers again, with no window to wait out.
mutation_finding: Nine mutants, nine killed on the first pass: the gate never gating, an unbounded queue, a slot never released, the queue timeout multiplied a thousandfold, one shared endpoint, a refusal that is a 500, the runtime keying every endpoint the same, the injected gate ignored, and the in-flight limit not read from the environment.
the_proof_found_my_own_script: The first end-to-end run parked for fifteen minutes on a request the server had in fact answered at thirty seconds; the server log showed the timeout firing on schedule. The hang was the proof script's `wait` in a non-interactive shell, not the product. The measurement was repeated with two slots and a wall clock: chat creation against a dead gateway took 30s and answered with no session, and the message was refused at exactly 30s with the gateway timeout message.
verification: Isolated instance, production build, a blackhole gateway that accepts every connection and never answers, gate limits 1 in flight and 0 queued: the second of two concurrent chat messages answered 503 'gateway gate saturated for http://127.0.0.1:8749: 1 in flight (limit 1), 0 queued (limit 0). The gateway is not keeping up; try again shortly.' Re-pointed at the healthy mock, a message answered 200. Gate by exit code: lint 0, tsc 0, 3872 tests / 437 suites, knip 0, canary OK, build 0.
